events.description: Investigate refractory hypokalemia: renal K/salt loss, hypertension, acid-base/endocrine evaluation

evidence.quote: The unexpectedly persistent and treatment-refractory hypokalemia prompted further investigation for underlying causes (Fig. 2) []. Urinalysis showed a markedly elevated urinary potassium-to-creatinine ratio (72.9 mEq/g), indicating renal potassium wasting. The patient’s blood pressure exceeded the 95th percentile plus 12 mmHg for age, meeting criteria for stage 2 hypertension per the 2017 American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines. This finding raised suspicion of renal or endocrine contributions to the electrolyte disturbance. Serum renin and aldosterone levels were within normal limits, ruling out hyperaldosteronism. Arterial blood gas revealed mild metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.48; HCO_(3)⁻ 24.7 mmol/L). A markedly elevated urinary chloride level (1,108 mmol/L) suggested renal salt loss. With no history of diuretic use and no clinical or laboratory evidence of Gitelman or Bartter syndrome, hypomagnesemia was considered the most likely underlying mechanism

summary.text: A 46-month-old girl had SRNS with renal-biopsy-confirmed minimal change disease and failure of full-dose prednisolone. Alternate-day prednisolone and CsA were followed by CsA dose escalation from 3.50 to 13.3 mg/kg/day over one year, maintained for several months before admission. The trough was 83 ng/mL within the stated 80–120 ng/mL therapeutic range. Adherence and no diuretic, aminoglycoside or other electrolyte-affecting exposure were documented.

On the second illness day she presented with one vomiting episode, two loose stools, fatigue, periorbital/lower-limb edema, weight 16 kg from 12 kg baseline and hypovolemic shock. Fluid resuscitation stabilized hemodynamics. Initial CBC, coagulation and liver panels and named sodium/chloride/calcium results were normal. Hypoalbuminemia 13.3 g/L, total protein 40.4 g/L, nephrotic-range urine protein 1.10 g/m²/day and UPCR 623 mg/mmol were documented. Ultrasound showed diffuse bowel edema and large simple ascites; both kidneys had normal size, increased cortical echogenicity and preserved corticomedullary differentiation.

Hypokalemia persisted despite resolution of vomiting/diarrhea and IV then oral potassium. Workup after nearly 10 days of poor response showed renal potassium wasting (urinary K/Cr 72.9 mEq/g), stage 2 hypertension, normal renin/aldosterone with hyperaldosteronism ruled out, mild metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.48, bicarbonate 24.7 mmol/L), and urine chloride 1,108 mmol/L suggesting renal salt loss. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of Gitelman or Bartter syndrome. Hypomagnesemia was initially considered the likely mechanism.

Sudden carpal tetany during blood-pressure measurement triggered the first magnesium draw on hospital day 10: 0.14 mmol/L with persistent hypokalemia and normal total/ionized calcium. Before tetany no overt weakness, tremor or diminished reflexes was observed. ECG remained normal without arrhythmias or QTc prolongation. FEMg could not be measured because urgent replacement and inability to provide urine prevented it, so renal magnesium loss was not confirmed.

IV magnesium sulfate resolved tetany within hours; repeat magnesium/potassium improved and eventually normalized. CsA was considered the likely etiology and temporarily held. Oral magnesium and four additional inpatient monitoring days brought stable clinical and biochemical improvement. After discharge, oral magnesium lactate with B6 continued for one week: 25 mg/kg/day as elemental magnesium, with each tablet containing 50 mg elemental magnesium and 5 mg B6; no potassium replacement was required. Electrolyte/CsA reassessment was scheduled. No completed outpatient visit or CsA restart was reported.
